newsitem.title: GERMANY: Thousands of miners gather in Bonn against cuts.
newsitem.headline: Thousands of miners gather in Bonn against cuts.

text.p: Thousands of angry German miners gathered in Bonn on Tuesday for protests against plans to cut coal subsidies as union leaders prepared to meet Chancellor Helmut Kohl in a last ditch attempt to reach a compromise.

Work in Germany's 18 pits ground to a halt on Friday after Bonn said it would cut subsidies to 3.8 billion marks ($2.2 billion) from nine billion by the year 2005. Miners accused the government of breaking a promise to phase out aid gradually.
Opposition Social Democrats (SPD) invited miners to sleep at the party's headquarters ahead of Tuesday's protest when union organisers expected up to 20,000 miners to converge on Bonn.
The SPD boycotted talks with the government on planned tax reforms last week in protest at the planned cuts, and said future cooperation would depend on the outcome of the meeting.
SPD parliamentary leader Rudolf Scharping addressed hundreds of miners at the party office and called the goverment plans a "death sentence" for the mining industry.

But Economics Minister Guenther Rexrodt said there was little room for compromise although he understood the worries of miners. "There is no way out of a drastic cut in subsidies in the next few years," Rexrodt told ARD television.

SPD party volunteers organised truckloads of sleeping bags and blankets and prepared hot food and drinks for demonstrators, who continued to block entrances to party buildings of the ruling coalition during the night.

The miners' union IG Bergbau says government plans will force 10 pits to close by 2005, make 50,000 of Germany's 90,000 miners redundant and cause a further 70,000 related job losses in already depressed areas.
While miners accept their industry's days are numbered, they argue that a minimum of 6.5 billion marks in subsidies until 2005 is essential to stem spiralling unemployment in mining regions.

In motorcycle convoys, cars and vans, 3,000 miners came to Bonn on Monday and blockaded a main road through the government quarter and the headquarters of Chancellor Helmut Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU) and the liberal Free Democrats (FDP).
Police were forced to turn traffic back just outside Kohl's Chancellory building.

Miners occupied town halls, pits and highways across Germany's Ruhr industrial heartland and Saar state on the French border. In Saar, tens of thousands miners blocked a motorway which is the country's main route to Luxembourg.

Chancellery Minister Friedrich Bohl said the government would stand firm by its "fair and comprehensive" offer. But miners cited a previous promise to maintain higher subsidies for longer and accused Bonn of going back on its word.

Miners, many clad in bright orange overalls and hard hats, sealed entrances to the FDP offices with chains on Monday, forcing it to move a weekly meeting to parliament buildings. The pro-market FDP are the driving force behind the cuts.
But FDP parliamentary economics spokesman Paul Friedhoff said he did not think Kohl would be moved by the protest.

"(IG Bergbau head Hans) Berger is speaking for 80,000 miners, Kohl for 80 million citizens, whose money must not be allowed to be used to finance unprofitable jobs any longer," Friedhoff told the Berliner Tageszeitung daily.
